Physically, with constant stiffness, a natural frequency tends to fall as mass increases, so under the weight conditions a downward shift of the peak frequency from the normal baseline is expected first. In the 1-0 condition, where the mass distribution is asymmetric, the change in the shape of the vibration response may appear in amplitude or band-energy features before it appears as a frequency shift.

The criterion for the model experiment is therefore not the absolute size of the compensation effect but whether the trend of improvement seen in openLAB (fewer false alarms after compensation) is reproduced in the same direction on our own system's data.

The main result plots — anomaly-score time series by condition, changes in the frequency spectrum, band-wise reconstruction-error contributions and so on — are presented in Figures 4–10. The +0.8% peak-frequency change in the 1-0 condition is opposite to the drop expected with added mass, but it is interpreted as a small change within the variation of manual excitation and the window-to-window fluctuation of the peak; the mass change of 1-0 was detected as an increase in the threshold-exceedance rate of the amplitude and band features (29.7%). By the rate of change in peak frequency, Δf = (f_condition − f_baseline) / f_baseline × 100 (%), the 1-1 condition showed a clear drop of −8.9%, while 1-0 was detected not by a frequency change but by changes in RMS, the band-energy features and the Autoencoder reconstruction error. This shows that even a low-cost MEMS sensor can detect changes in dynamic properties due to changes in mass distribution. On a small foam-board model, however, differences in manual excitation, the sensor's fixing and cable movement may affect the natural frequency more than temperature and humidity do, so the temperature/humidity-compensation effect was not concluded from the model experiment alone but cross-checked against the openLAB analysis in 2.7; the result is reflected in the difference in exceedance rates between the uncompensated and temperature/humidity-compensated models.

r1-p14-005: This work collected vibration and temperature/humidity data from a model bridge with a low-cost device consisting of an ADXL355Z accelerometer, a DHT22 sensor and a Raspberry Pi 3 Model A+, and checked whether the peak frequency, RMS, band energies and Autoencoder reconstruction error change under changes in mass distribution. After compensating for environmental effects with a temperature/humidity multivariate regression learned on normal data and judging anomalies by reconstruction error, the F1 score improved about 4.9-fold, from 0.075 uncompensated to 0.370, and the false-alarm rate in the normal segment where only humidity changed fell by nearly half, from 17.5% to 9.1%. Because manual excitation and the sensor's fixing also affect the model bridge, however, the temperature/humidity-compensation effect is interpreted cautiously, together with the openLAB analysis.
r1-p14-006: This improvement involves a trade-off. The false-alarm rate over all normal windows with environmental variation fell from 0.092 uncompensated to 0.048 with temperature compensation and then rose slightly to 0.063 with temperature/humidity compensation, while recall rose from 0.197 to 0.234, greatly improving F1, and precision on the damage conditions stayed high at about 0.89. By condition, in 1-1, with 100 g added on each side, the first peak frequency fell by 8.9%, so the large mass change clearly appeared as a resonance shift. In 1-0, with 100 g on one side only, the frequency change was only 0.8%, but the asymmetric mass made the response irregular, giving the highest anomalous-window rate, 29.7%, while 1-1 was actually lower at 18.8% as the first mode settled into a new resonance. Even in the normal condition 0-0 the anomalous-window rate remained at 4.5%, so false alarms did not disappear completely. In short, the system behaves as a first-stage screening tool: when it alarms, an actual anomaly is likely (high precision), but it catches only about 23% of all anomalies. Given these characteristics, the system is a supplementary means for aging small and medium bridges short of inspection staff and budget, using low-cost sensors to pick out suspect sections first and set precision-inspection priorities, and it serves as a selective early-warning means of anomaly risk rather than a replacement for precision safety diagnosis. Because the node is built from inexpensive general-purpose parts and is easy to distribute across many bridges, allocating inspection resources first to bridges where anomaly candidates and main contributing bands reported by each node accumulate can fill, at the level of continuous screening, the time gap between inspection cycles raised in 1.1.
r1-p14-007: What distinguishes this work from existing research lies in the form of the outcome. Its contribution is not only an analysis result obtained by applying an algorithm to public data, but the direct implementation of low-cost sensor-based data collection, environmental compensation, anomaly judgment and band-wise explanation as one measurement-and-analysis
r1-p15-000: pipeline. Vibration and temperature/humidity measurement, environmental compensation, anomaly judgment and band-contribution explanation were integrated into a single device that works at the measurement site, implemented and demonstrated directly; unlike fiber-optic BOCDA measurement, which precisely measures local deformation with dedicated infrastructure, it aims at low-cost screening applicable to small and medium aging bridges in general. It is also distinguished by explaining not just whether there is an anomaly but which frequency band departed from the normal baseline. Analysis of the long-term monitoring data of Germany's openLAB, public data from a full-scale bridge, was performed as a reference validation of this environmental-compensation method, and its results are presented in 2.7. It confirmed that environmental compensation reduces false alarms on real-bridge data with accumulated seasonal change and daily temperature ranges, and our own model-bridge experiment confirmed that the same pipeline reproduces a similar trend of improvement.
r1-p15-002: This study identified three limitations. First, the foam-board model has high damping, so vibration dies out quickly and the first mode is unstable, making it hard to detect the small mass change of the 1-0 condition, with 100 g on one side only, as a frequency change. Second, the manual method of pressing and releasing with a finger applied vibration with inconsistent force and timing, increasing the variability of the data. Third, the range of temperature change that could be created indoors was small, limiting the effect of temperature-only compensation. Together these limitations kept damage-detection recall at about 0.23 even after compensation. The limitation of temperature range was supplemented by the openLAB analysis in 2.7, but that is offline validation, so follow-up research needs to extend the public-data analysis while improving our own system's excitation method, sensor layout and model structure to make real measurement data more stable. On this basis, three directions of improvement are planned. First, improve the model and experimental conditions. Replacing the foam board with aluminum beams removes the excessive damping and secures a stable first natural frequency, which can raise sensitivity and recall for small mass changes. Tapping automatically at a constant force and interval with a solenoid auto-tapper instead of a finger reduces input variation, narrows the feature distribution of normal data and makes the separation between normal and anomalous sharper. On this foundation, the experiment will be extended in three directions: finding the smallest detectable mass change with finer weight steps, examining the possibility of damage localization by dividing the model into sections, and verifying the compensation effect over a wider range of temperature and humidity. The goal of this stage is to show the halving of the humidity-segment false-alarm rate seen here (17.5% to 9.1%) in a clearer and more reproducible form.
r1-p15-003: Second, install the system on a real bridge in service for long-term field validation. A real bridge uses the ambient vibration produced by vehicles and wind as is, so no separate exciter or traffic closure is needed. Attaching measurement nodes to the deck or girders and collecting vibration and temperature/humidity continuously for weeks to months would let our own sensors directly observe the temperature–natural-frequency relationship that repeats daily and seasonally, quantify the reduction in false alarms from temperature/humidity compensation over a long period, and also test practical issues such as the durability of sensor mounting and the stability of power and storage.
r1-p15-004: Third, extend measurement beyond a single node to multiple nodes. With nodes at several points on a bridge, comparing responses between points makes it possible to examine the localization of anomalies, and collecting measurement data remotely could develop the system into a management tool that compares the anomaly scores of many bridges on one screen to help set precision-inspection priorities. In long-term operation, however, the baseline may drift because of sensor drift and similar effects, so a procedure for periodically retraining on normal data and updating the threshold is needed.
